context.heading: Steering, not just knowing
context.body: The wise gain tachbulot ("guidance"), a word probably linked to the ropes a sailor pulls to steer a ship. In Proverbs it means skill at navigating choices, not a stock of facts. Hebrew wisdom is practical: knowing how to live well in God's world, the way a craftsman knows his trade.

context.heading: Throwing in your lot
context.body: The gang says, "Throw in your goral ("lot") with us; we will all share one purse." A lot was the token used to divide land and plunder. They offer more than money: belonging, a shared fund, a new identity. Ancient roads had real bandits who ambushed travelers, so the warning was not abstract.

context.heading: Wisdom in the town square
context.body: Wisdom does not whisper in a temple; she shouts in the street, the square and at the city gate (vv. 20–21), where business, lawsuits and gossip happened. Her speech sounds like a prophet's, with "how long" and warnings of disaster. Wisdom is public, available to anyone willing to stop and listen.

theology.title: Wisdom starts with a Person
theology.body: Verse 7 makes knowledge depend on a relationship: the fear of the LORD, using God's covenant name. Proverbs does not treat wisdom as clever technique but as living rightly before the God who made the world. Paul says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ (Colossians 2:3).

theology.title: Patient, then honest
theology.body: Wisdom calls again and again before she warns (vv. 22–27). When people refuse, they "eat the fruit of their way" (v. 31). God often judges by handing people over to the results of their own choices, as Paul describes in Romans 1:24. His patience is real, but it is not indifference.

theology.title: A rejected voice
theology.body: Wisdom pours out her spirit and makes her words known (v. 23), then is refused by the very people she calls. Jesus, the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), wept over Jerusalem: "How often I have longed to gather your children together" (Matthew 23:37). God's wisdom has always been a voice calling out, not a secret withheld.

application.title: The pitch is belonging
application.body: The gang never says "come do evil." They say "come with us" and "we will all share one purse" (vv. 11, 14). Most bad choices are sold as friendship.
application.question: Which group in your life makes it easiest to do what you already know is wrong?

application.title: Nets in plain sight
application.body: Verse 17 notes that a bird sees the net and flies in anyway, and verse 18 says the gang is really ambushing its own lives. Greed blinds people to traps they can plainly see.
application.question: Where are you chasing a gain you can already tell will cost more than it pays?

application.title: How long?
application.body: Wisdom asks the simple how long they will love being simple (v. 22). Staying uncommitted can feel safe, but drifting is still a direction.
application.question: What decision have you been putting off because not deciding feels easier?

context.heading: Outside the covenant
context.body: The BSB's "forbidden woman" translates zarah, literally "strange" or "outsider," paired with a word for "foreign woman" (BSB "stranger"). The point is not ethnicity but someone outside your covenant, a person who belongs to another marriage. She has left "the partner of her youth" (v. 17), so the danger is betrayal on both sides.

context.heading: Wisdom that works
context.body: God stores up tushiyyah ("sound wisdom") for the upright. The word carries the sense of effective, lasting success: practical good sense that actually holds when life tests it. It is treasure God keeps in reserve, the way a king keeps a storehouse for hard times.

context.heading: Ruts in the road
context.body: Ma'gal ("path") is a wagon track, the ruts worn into ancient roads by repeated travel. Wisdom helps you see which tracks lead somewhere good. Habits work the same way: the more often a way is taken, the deeper the groove and the easier the next trip down it.

theology.title: Gift and pursuit together
theology.body: Verses 1–4 tell the son to seek and dig; verse 6 says, "the LORD gives wisdom." Scripture holds both without strain. God is generous, and He gives most richly to those who actually want what He gives. James 1:5 makes the same promise to anyone who asks.

theology.title: God as bodyguard
theology.body: God is a shield to the upright (v. 7), guards the paths of justice and protects the way of His faithful ones (v. 8). "Faithful ones," chasidim, comes from chesed, His covenant love. His protection here is not luck; it flows from His loyalty to people bound to Him.

theology.title: Who inherits the land
theology.body: The upright will live in the land, while the wicked are uprooted (vv. 21–22). This echoes Psalm 37:9–11, and Jesus widens it: "Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5). God's promise of a home runs from Canaan to the new creation.

application.title: Effort reveals value
application.body: People dig for silver because they believe it is worth something. How hard you search shows what you actually value, whatever you say you value.
application.question: What do the last seven days of your time and attention say you are digging for?

application.title: Smooth words
application.body: The adulteress is marked by flattering words (v. 16). Temptation rarely starts with a body; it usually starts with someone telling you what you want to hear about yourself.
application.question: Whose flattery do you find yourself seeking out when you feel unappreciated?

application.title: Bigger than feelings
application.body: She forgot the covenant of her God (v. 17), not just a spouse. Promises made before God stay binding when the feelings that came with them change.
application.question: Which commitment are you treating as optional because it no longer feels the way it did when you made it?

context.heading: Love and truth as a necklace
context.body: Chesed ("loving devotion") and emet ("faithfulness") are the pair God uses to describe Himself in Exodus 34:6. The son is to bind them around his neck and write them on his heart, like the reminders of Deuteronomy 6:8. God's own character becomes the jewelry His people wear.

context.heading: The first, not the leftovers
context.body: Reshit ("firstfruits") was the first and best of the harvest, given to God before anyone knew how big the crop would be (Exodus 23:19). That made it an act of trust. The promise of full barns and overflowing vats (v. 10) speaks in the language of a farmer's year.

context.heading: What is already owed
context.body: Verse 27 literally says not to withhold good from its "owners," using ba'al. A neighbor's wage or help is treated as already belonging to him. Day laborers were to be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:15), so "come back tomorrow" (v. 28) could mean a family went hungry that night.

theology.title: Wisdom built the world
theology.body: The LORD founded the earth by wisdom and set the heavens in place by understanding (vv. 19–20). The same wisdom offered to the son holds the universe together. Living wisely means living with the grain of how God made things, the world Paul says was made through and holds together in Christ (Colossians 1:16–17).

theology.title: The tree of life again
theology.body: Wisdom is called a tree of life (v. 18), the tree Adam and Eve were barred from after the fall (Genesis 3:22–24). Proverbs hints that something lost in Eden can be tasted again through wisdom. Revelation 22:2 shows the tree restored in full for God's people.

theology.title: Grace to the humble
theology.body: God mocks the mockers but gives grace to the humble (v. 34). James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 both quote this verse from the Greek Old Testament. Humility is not low self-esteem; it is the open hand that can receive what God gives.

application.title: Pay it today
application.body: Verse 28 forbids telling a neighbor to come back tomorrow when you can help now. Delay feels neutral to the one delaying, but to the one waiting it is a decision.
application.question: Who is waiting on something from you this week that you could settle today?

application.title: Needless fights
application.body: Verse 30 warns against accusing someone who has done you no harm. Picking fights, online or at home, is often a way of venting pressure that has nothing to do with the other person.
application.question: What was really behind the last argument you started?

application.title: Envy of the ruthless
application.body: Verse 31 says not to envy a violent man or choose any of his ways. Envy is sneaky: you can despise someone's methods and still want their results.
application.question: Whose success do you secretly want even though you would never do what they did to get it?

context.heading: Brighter toward noon
context.body: The path of the righteous is like the nogah ("first gleam") of dawn, shining brighter until full day. In the Judean hills, first light grows steadily into blazing midday. Growth in wisdom is pictured as gradual and real, not instant and not finished all at once.

context.heading: Weigh the path
context.body: Palas ("make level") can also mean to weigh, as on a balance. The father asks the son to consider where each step lands, smoothing the road and testing it before walking. Wise living means examining your path, not just reacting to whatever comes next.

context.heading: Living on violence
context.body: The wicked "eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence" (v. 17). In a culture where bread and wine were daily survival, the image is sharp: harming others has become their regular diet. Verse 16 adds that they cannot sleep until they have made someone stumble.

theology.title: Faith handed down
theology.body: God's wisdom travels through families: David to Solomon to Solomon's son, just as Deuteronomy 6:7 told parents to teach at home and on the road. God works through ordinary teaching at kitchen tables. Paul saw the same pattern in Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5).

theology.title: The spring needs renewing
theology.body: Jesus said evil thoughts and actions come out of the heart (Mark 7:21–23), the same place verse 23 calls the source of life. Guarding alone cannot clean a polluted spring. That is why God promises a new heart and a new spirit, not just better behavior (Ezekiel 36:26).

theology.title: Light that keeps growing
theology.body: The brightening path (v. 18) fits the whole story of Scripture: God moves His people from darkness toward full day. Paul says believers are being transformed from glory to glory (2 Corinthians 3:18), and Revelation 22:5 ends with no need for any lamp, because God Himself is their light.

application.title: What is flowing in
application.body: If life flows out of the heart (v. 23), what you let in matters. Feeds, shows and conversations are not neutral; they are slowly shaping the spring.
application.question: What one input would you cut this week if you took verse 23 seriously?

application.title: Eyes forward
application.body: Verse 25 tells you to let your eyes look straight ahead. Drift usually starts with a glance at what is off the path, then a longer look.
application.question: Where do your eyes tend to wander when you are tired or bored?

application.title: Someone is learning from you
application.body: The father teaches what his own father taught him. Whatever faith you have, someone is watching how you actually live it.
application.question: Who is learning from you right now, and what are they really learning?

context.heading: Honey, then wormwood
context.body: Her lips drip honey (v. 3), but in the end she is bitter as la'anah ("wormwood"), a plant known for its harsh taste. The contrast is between first impression and final outcome. The prophets used wormwood for the bitterness of judgment (Jeremiah 9:15).

context.heading: Tied with his own rope
context.body: The wicked man is held fast by the chevel ("cords") of his own sin. Hunters used ropes and snares to catch animals, but here no hunter is needed. The man weaves the rope himself, one choice at a time, until he cannot get free.

context.heading: The cost in public
context.body: Verse 14 says ruin came "in the midst of the whole assembly." In a small Israelite town, adultery touched property, family honor and legal standing, and could be judged before the community. The father counts the costs: honor, years, strength and labor handed to strangers (vv. 9–10).

theology.title: God sees every path
theology.body: The ways of a man are before the LORD, who examines all his paths (v. 21). Nothing done in secret is hidden from Him (Hebrews 4:13). That is a warning to the unfaithful, and a comfort to anyone who has been betrayed: the wrong done to them is fully seen.

theology.title: Sex as a gift, not a threat
theology.body: Verses 18–19 tell a husband to rejoice in his wife and be delighted by her love. The Bible does not treat sexuality as shameful but as a good gift guarded by covenant, from Genesis 2:24 to the Song of Songs. Paul builds on the same picture of mutual love in 1 Corinthians 7:3–5.

theology.title: Sin carries its own sentence
theology.body: God built a moral order into reality, so sin often traps the sinner (v. 22). This does not mean God is absent; it means He made a world where actions have real consequences. Galatians 6:7 says the same: whatever a person sows, he will also reap.

application.title: Drift is often unaware
application.body: She does not consider the path of life; her ways wander and she does not even know it (v. 6). Most betrayals begin with small choices that feel like nothing at the time.
application.question: What small step are you taking that you would not want the people who trust you to see?

application.title: Regret's script
application.body: Verses 12–13 give the words of someone looking back: "How I hated discipline!" The father hands his son this script now so he never has to say it.
application.question: What warning are you brushing off that you suspect you will one day wish you had heeded?

application.title: Delight on purpose
application.body: "Rejoice in the wife of your youth" is a command (v. 18). In a long marriage or any lasting friendship, delight is something you cultivate, not something you wait to feel.
application.question: What would it look like this week to pursue joy in your closest relationship instead of waiting for it?

context.heading: Humble yourself
context.body: If you are trapped by a pledge, go and "humble yourself," raphas, a verb meaning to stamp or trample down, perhaps picturing someone lowering himself before his neighbor. The advice is urgent: no sleep until you are free (v. 4). Pride should not keep you stuck in a bad promise.

context.heading: A good-for-nothing
context.body: The "worthless person" is literally a man of beliyya'al, "without worth." The word later became a name for wickedness itself, and Paul uses Belial for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). This man winks, signals with his feet and points with his fingers (v. 13), working by secret codes.

context.heading: No price will settle it
context.body: Qin'ah ("jealousy") here is a wronged husband's fury. A thief who steals bread can repay sevenfold (v. 31), but adultery cannot be paid off; no ransom will satisfy (v. 35). The law treated adultery as a capital crime (Leviticus 20:10), showing how seriously Israel took marriage.

theology.title: What God hates
theology.body: The LORD hates pride, lies, violence, scheming, eagerness for evil, false witness and stirring up conflict among brothers (vv. 16–19). Almost every item is a sin against community. God's hatred is not irritability; it is His love for people opposing what destroys them.

theology.title: Discord matters to God
theology.body: The list climaxes with the one who sows discord among brothers. Jesus prayed that His followers would be one (John 17:21), and Paul urged the church to keep the unity of the Spirit (Ephesians 4:3). Splitting God's people is not a small sin in His eyes.

theology.title: Adultery starts within
theology.body: Verse 25 warns, "Do not lust in your heart after her beauty." Jesus taught the same: looking with lust is adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28). God's standard reaches past behavior to desire, which is why He offers new hearts, not just new rules.

application.title: Careful what you sign
application.body: Verses 1–5 warn against guaranteeing someone else's debt. Co-signing a loan or making a large promise can feel kind in the moment and wreck a relationship later.
application.question: What financial or time commitment have you made that you need to go back and renegotiate?

application.title: Just a little sleep
application.body: The sluggard never decides to fail; he just takes a little sleep, a little slumber (v. 10). Poverty arrives like a robber, not all at once but certainly.
application.question: Where are you hitting snooze on something that keeps getting more expensive?

application.title: Discord in the group chat
application.body: The last sin on God's list is stirring up strife among brothers. A forwarded screenshot or a "just between us" comment can do it in seconds.
application.question: What conversation are you part of that is quietly turning people against each other?

context.heading: The little man in your eye
context.body: Keep my teaching as the ishon ("apple") of your eye, literally the "little man" of the eye, the pupil where you see your own reflection. You protect your pupil by instinct. The same word returns in verse 9: the young man walks out in the "pupil" of the night, its darkest center.

context.heading: All of a sudden
context.body: He follows her pit'om ("suddenly" or "on impulse"). After a long, slow drift through the streets, the final choice happens in a moment. He goes like an ox to slaughter or a bird into a snare, not knowing it will cost his life (v. 23).

context.heading: Call wisdom your sister
context.body: Say to wisdom, "You are my achot ("sister")." In the Song of Songs, "sister" is a term of close affection between lovers (Song 4:9). The father offers wisdom as the true companion who can stand between his son and the woman's smooth words.

theology.title: God's word as protection
theology.body: The answer to temptation in verses 1–5 is not willpower but God's commands kept close, bound on the fingers and written on the heart. Jesus answered each of Satan's temptations with Scripture (Matthew 4:1–11). Jeremiah 31:33 promises a covenant where God writes His law on hearts.

theology.title: Religion as a cover
theology.body: She has offered sacrifices and paid her vows (v. 14), then uses the meal to set up sin. God has always rejected worship used to cover wrongdoing (Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24). He wants hearts that match the ritual, not rituals that hide the heart.

theology.title: Roads have destinations
theology.body: Her house is the road to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death (v. 27). Scripture keeps describing two ways with two ends (Psalm 1; Matthew 7:13–14). God tells us plainly where roads lead because He wants us to arrive home.

application.title: Where you walk
application.body: He went near her corner and strolled toward her house (v. 8). He did not plan to sin; he just put himself where sin was easy.
application.question: Where do you keep ending up that makes your worst choices easy?

application.title: When no one is home
application.body: Her husband is away on a long journey (vv. 19–20). Temptation often waits for moments when accountability is absent: travel, late nights, empty houses.
application.question: What guardrail do you need for the times when no one would ever know?

application.title: Flattery feels like being seen
application.body: She seized him, kissed him and told him she came out looking for him (vv. 13–15). Being sought out is powerful when you feel invisible.
application.question: What unmet need makes you most vulnerable to someone who says exactly what you want to hear?

context.heading: Marking the horizon
context.body: God inscribed a chug ("circle") on the face of the deep. To an observer at sea, the horizon looks like a circle where sky meets water. The image is a builder drawing lines with a compass, setting limits so the sea stays where God put it (v. 29).

context.heading: Playing before Him
context.body: Wisdom was "rejoicing" before God, sachaq, a verb that can mean to laugh or play. Creation is pictured not as grim labor but as joyful work, with Wisdom delighting at God's side. Verse 31 adds that her sha'ashu'im ("delight") was in the human race.

context.heading: Better than silver
context.body: Wisdom says her instruction is worth more than silver, gold and jewels (vv. 10–11, 19). In Solomon's day silver was so plentiful in Jerusalem it was considered of little value (1 Kings 10:21, 27). Even that kind of wealth could not buy what Wisdom offers.

theology.title: Christ, the wisdom of God
theology.body: The New Testament uses this chapter's language for Christ: the Word was with God in the beginning and all things were made through Him (John 1:1–3); He is before all things (Colossians 1:15–17). Christians confess the Son as eternal, not created, and read Proverbs 8 as poetry that prepares for Him.

theology.title: God delights in people
theology.body: Wisdom's joy at creation ends in delight in mankind (v. 31). God did not make humans reluctantly. Before the fall there was delight, and Scripture keeps returning to it: "The LORD your God... will rejoice over you with singing" (Zephaniah 3:17).

theology.title: Life is found in Him
theology.body: "Whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD" (v. 35). Jesus says, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). Wisdom is not just good advice; it is the road to life itself, and missing it harms the soul (v. 36).

application.title: Wisdom shouts
application.body: Wisdom calls at the crossroads and the city gates (vv. 1–3), the busiest places in town. God's truth is not hidden in obscure corners for spiritual experts.
application.question: Where in your busy routine are you tuning out a voice that is calling plainly?

application.title: Comfortable with what God hates
application.body: The fear of the LORD is to hate evil, pride, arrogance and perverse speech (v. 13). It is possible to love God in theory and feel quite at home with the things He hates.
application.question: Which kind of pride or twisted speech have you grown comfortable with?

application.title: Waiting at the door
application.body: Blessed is the one who listens, watching daily at Wisdom's doors (v. 34). The picture is someone who shows up every day expecting something.
application.question: What would change if you came to Scripture each day like someone waiting for a door to open?

context.heading: Woman Folly
context.body: Kesilut ("folly") is pictured as a loud, ignorant woman sitting at her door. Unlike Wisdom, she has built nothing, prepared nothing and sent out no servants. She sits at the highest point of the city calling to whoever passes, copying Wisdom's invitation word for word (v. 16).

context.heading: A prepared feast
context.body: Wisdom has masakh ("mixed") her wine. Wine was mixed with water or spices to make it fit for a banquet. It signals a carefully prepared feast, where the host has thought of every detail for her guests before sending out the invitations.

context.heading: The Holy One
context.body: Knowledge of the qedoshim ("Holy One") is understanding. The Hebrew is plural, likely a plural of majesty that intensifies God's holiness. Verse 10 repeats the theme of 1:7, so the fear of the LORD brackets all of chapters 1 to 9.

theology.title: The gospel banquet
theology.body: Wisdom sends out servants to invite the simple to her feast (vv. 3–5). Jesus told parables of a king's banquet with servants sent to call guests from the streets (Matthew 22:1–10; Luke 14:16–24). Isaiah 55:1 sounds the same call: come, buy wine and milk without money.

theology.title: Holy, not just bigger
theology.body: The Holy One (v. 10) is the God whose holiness the seraphim proclaim (Isaiah 6:3). Wisdom begins with knowing God as utterly different, pure and set apart, not a larger version of ourselves. Fear of the LORD grows from seeing Him as He is.

theology.title: Two destinies
theology.body: Wisdom's guests gain years of life (v. 11); Folly's guests are in the depths of Sheol (v. 18). The choice is between life and death, as Moses set before Israel (Deuteronomy 30:19). God makes the stakes clear because He wants people to choose life.

application.title: How you take correction
application.body: Rebuke a mocker and he will hate you; rebuke a wise man and he will love you (v. 8). Your reaction to correction says more about you than about the person correcting.
application.question: Whose correction are you still resenting, and what would it look like to receive it as a gift?

application.title: Secrecy as flavor
application.body: "Stolen water is sweet" (v. 17). Some sins attract us mainly because they are hidden, and the secret itself is the thrill.
application.question: What do you enjoy partly because no one knows about it?

application.title: No one else pays
application.body: If you are wise, it benefits you; if you mock, you alone will bear it (v. 12). No one else can carry the result of your choices for you.
application.question: Which choice are you making as if someone else will absorb the cost?

context.heading: Many words, crossed lines
context.body: When words are many, pesha ("transgression") is not absent. Pesha is a strong word, used for rebellion and breaking covenant. The proverb is not just saying talkers make mistakes; it says excessive talk tends to cross real moral lines.

context.heading: Blessing without the grind
context.body: The LORD's blessing brings wealth, and He adds no etsev ("sorrow" or "painful toil") to it. Etsev echoes the curse in Genesis 3:16–17, where painful toil enters human life. God's blessing quietly pushes back against that curse.

context.heading: After the storm
context.body: When the suphah ("whirlwind") passes, the wicked are gone, but the righteous stand firm forever. Sudden storms swept off the Mediterranean and through the wadis of Israel. Jesus told of two builders, one on rock and one on sand, whose houses faced the same storm (Matthew 7:24–27).

theology.title: The LORD is for His people
theology.body: The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry (v. 3), His way is a stronghold for the upright (v. 29), and fearing Him adds length to life (v. 27). Christians differ on whether to read such sayings as promises or as general principles. Either way, they reveal a God who is for His people and against injustice.

theology.title: A blessed memory
theology.body: "The memory of the righteous is a blessing" (v. 7). God keeps a book of remembrance for those who fear Him (Malachi 3:16), and the deeds of those who die in the Lord follow them (Revelation 14:13). Nothing done in faith is forgotten by Him.

theology.title: Words that feed
theology.body: The lips of the righteous feed many (v. 21). God is a God who speaks, and His people's words are meant to nourish others. Jesus said we live by every word that comes from God's mouth (Matthew 4:4), and He gives us words to share.

application.title: Talk less
application.body: Verse 19 says whoever restrains his lips is wise. Fewer words means fewer regrets, fewer confidences broken and more room to listen.
application.question: In which conversation this week did you say more than you needed to?

application.title: Harvest time
application.body: A wise son gathers in summer; a disgraceful son sleeps through harvest (v. 5). Some opportunities have a season, and once it passes it does not return.
application.question: What season of opportunity in your life right now are you sleeping through?

application.title: Hidden hatred
application.body: Whoever conceals hatred has lying lips (v. 18). You can be polite to someone while privately despising them, and that is a lie too.
application.question: Who are you being pleasant to while resentment keeps growing underneath?

context.heading: Gold in the mud
context.body: A nezem ("ring") was a gold nose ring, valued jewelry for women in the ancient world (Genesis 24:47). Pigs were unclean animals in Israel, rooting in mud and garbage. Beauty without discretion is a precious thing wasted, carried around by something that drags it through the dirt.

context.heading: Scattering seed
context.body: One person gives pazar ("freely," literally "scatters") and yet gains even more. The verb pictures a farmer flinging seed across a field. A farmer who refuses to throw good grain on the ground keeps it safe, but he never sees a harvest.

context.heading: Quiet modesty
context.body: With tsanua ("humility") comes wisdom. The word is rare, appearing elsewhere only in Micah 6:8, "walk humbly with your God." It suggests a quiet, modest way of carrying yourself, the opposite of the pride that brings disgrace in the first half of the verse.

theology.title: God in the marketplace
theology.body: A dishonest scale is detestable to the LORD (v. 1). His concern for honest business runs through the law and the prophets (Leviticus 19:35–36; Amos 8:5). For God, worship cannot be separated from how you treat a customer or an employer on Monday.

theology.title: The generosity paradox
theology.body: The generous will prosper, and whoever refreshes others will be refreshed (v. 25). Paul applies the same principle: "Whoever sows generously will also reap generously" (2 Corinthians 9:6). God built a world where giving, in the long run, does not make His people poorer.

theology.title: Righteousness blesses a city
theology.body: When the righteous thrive, the city rejoices; by their blessing a city is lifted up (vv. 10–11). God places His people in communities to bless them, as He told the exiles in Babylon to seek the peace of the city where He sent them (Jeremiah 29:7).

application.title: Your scales today
application.body: Dishonest scales today look like padded invoices, fudged expense reports or hours rounded up. God cares about these as much as about Sunday worship.
application.question: Where do you have a quiet habit of tilting the scale your way?

application.title: Hoarding hurts neighbors
application.body: People curse the one who holds back grain to drive up the price (v. 26). Hoarding in hard times turns a shortage into someone else's crisis.
application.question: What are you holding tightly that someone near you badly needs?

application.title: Looks without judgment
application.body: Verse 22 applies to anyone: appearance, talent or charm without good judgment is wasted. We spend far more on how we look than on how we choose.
application.question: Which part of your life gets more attention for how it looks than for how wise it is?

context.heading: Like a dumb animal
context.body: Whoever hates correction is ba'ar ("stupid"), a word related to livestock that simply graze. The point is not low intelligence but an animal-like refusal to learn. Psalm 73:22 uses the same word when the psalmist admits, "I was a brute beast before You."

context.heading: A strong wife
context.body: A wife of chayil ("noble character") is her husband's crown. Chayil means strength, valor or capability, the same word that opens the poem in 31:10. In a culture where a household was a small business and farm, a capable wife was central to its survival.

context.heading: The weight of worry
context.body: De'agah ("anxiety") in a person's heart weighs it down, but a good word cheers it up. The picture is someone bowed under a load. Proverbs treats anxiety as real and heavy, and it also recognizes the power of a kind word to lift it.

theology.title: God loves truth
theology.body: Lying lips are detestable to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are His delight (v. 22). God's own nature is truth: He does not lie (Numbers 23:19), and Jesus calls Himself the truth (John 14:6). His people reflect Him when their word can be trusted.

theology.title: God cares for animals
theology.body: The righteous man knows the needs of his animal (v. 10). God feeds the birds (Matthew 6:26), gave animals Sabbath rest (Exodus 23:12) and cared about Nineveh's cattle (Jonah 4:11). His goodness reaches every creature, and His people are meant to show the same care.

theology.title: Life beyond the path
theology.body: "There is life in the path of righteousness" (v. 28). The second line is hard to translate: the BSB reads "another path leads to death," while others read "along its path there is no death." If the latter is right, it is one of the Old Testament's hints of life beyond the grave, which Christ brought fully to light (2 Timothy 1:10).

application.title: Rash words linger
application.body: Reckless words pierce like a sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing (v. 18). One cutting comment can stay with someone for years after you have forgotten it.
application.question: Who might still be carrying a wound from something careless you said?

application.title: One good word
application.body: Verse 25 says a good word can lift an anxious heart. You do not have to fix someone's problem to help them carry it.
application.question: Who around you is weighed down right now, and what could you say to them today?

application.title: Image versus reality
application.body: Verse 9 says it is better to be unimportant and have what you need than to act important and go without food. Our culture rewards looking successful over being stable.
application.question: What are you spending to look like something you are not?

context.heading: Wealth from vapor
context.body: Dishonest wealth dwindles away; the Hebrew is literally wealth from hevel ("vapor" or "breath"), the word that runs through Ecclesiastes. Money gained from nothing, by scheme or hype, tends to vanish like breath on a cold day. Wealth gathered little by little grows.

context.heading: Up early for your child
context.body: The one who loves his son disciplines him shachar ("diligently"), a verb linked to dawn and meaning to seek early or eagerly. The stress falls on an attentive parent who cares enough to act early, not on harshness. Love gets up early to deal with problems while they are small.

context.heading: Walking together
context.body: Whoever halakh ("walks") with the wise grows wise. In Hebrew, walking describes a whole way of life, as Enoch walked with God (Genesis 5:24). The second line holds a wordplay: the companion (ro'eh) of fools will suffer harm (yeroa').

theology.title: A fountain of life
theology.body: The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, turning a person away from the snares of death (v. 14). Jeremiah calls God Himself the fountain of living water (Jeremiah 2:13), and Jesus offers water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life (John 4:10–14).

theology.title: God fulfills hope
theology.body: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a longing fulfilled is a tree of life (v. 12). God does not ask us to pretend that delay does not hurt. Romans 5:5 says hope in Him does not put us to shame, because His love has been poured into our hearts.

theology.title: Justice on a longer clock
theology.body: A good man leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren, but the sinner's wealth is stored up for the righteous (v. 22). God's justice often works across generations, not on our timeline. Psalm 37 gives the same counsel: do not fret, wait for the LORD.

application.title: Your closest three
application.body: Walk with the wise and you will become wise (v. 20). You become like the people you spend the most time with, usually without noticing.
application.question: If you became exactly like your three closest friends, would that be good news?

application.title: Fast money
application.body: Money gained in a hurry tends to vanish (v. 11). Pump-and-dump coins, betting apps and too-good-to-be-true side hustles all sell the same promise.
application.question: What shortcut to money are you tempted by right now?

application.title: Guard your mouth
application.body: Whoever guards his mouth protects his life (v. 3). Not every thought needs to be spoken, posted or texted.
application.question: What would you stop saying if you knew it would be repeated word for word?

context.heading: Grief no one else can enter
context.body: The heart knows its own morrah ("bitterness"), and no stranger shares its joy. Some grief and some gladness cannot be fully explained to anyone else. Proverbs honors that inner solitude without pretending a clever saying can fix it.

context.heading: Grace and disgrace
context.body: Sin is a "disgrace" to any people. The Hebrew word here is chesed, usually "loving devotion," but in this verse it carries a rare second meaning, "reproach" or "shame." The same letters can name God's loyal love or a nation's shame, a jarring contrast.

context.heading: A messy barn
context.body: Where there are no oxen, the evus ("manger") is empty, but from the strength of an ox comes an abundant harvest. Oxen are messy and need feeding and constant care. A farmer who wants a clean barn and no work will also have no crop.

theology.title: God stands with the poor
theology.body: Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, and whoever is kind to the needy honors Him (v. 31). Jesus took this to its fullest: whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for Me (Matthew 25:40). Every person bears God's image.

theology.title: A refuge for children
theology.body: In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence, and His children will have a refuge (v. 26). Faith in God is not only private; it shapes the security of a whole family. God is called a refuge again and again in Scripture (Psalm 46:1).

theology.title: The one right way
theology.body: A way can seem right and still end in death (v. 12). Judges 21:25 describes Israel's chaos when everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Jesus does not just point to the right road; He says He Himself is the way that leads to life (John 14:6).

application.title: Fruitful is messy
application.body: Verse 4 says an empty manger is clean but fruitless. Kids, ministry, a growing business and real friendships all make a mess.
application.question: What good thing are you avoiding because it would complicate your tidy life?

application.title: Laughter over grief
application.body: Even in laughter the heart may ache (v. 13). The friend who jokes the most is sometimes the one hurting the most.
application.question: Who in your life might be hiding pain behind humor?

application.title: Quick to react
application.body: A quick-tempered person acts foolishly, while patience shows great understanding (vv. 17, 29). The faster your reactions, the less wisdom they usually contain.
application.question: What situation keeps setting off your fastest and worst reactions?

context.heading: Even the underworld is open
context.body: Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD. Abaddon means "destruction" and names the deepest realm of the dead (Job 26:6); Revelation 9:11 uses it as the name of the angel of the abyss. If the underworld is open to God, how much more human hearts.

context.heading: A plain bowl of vegetables
context.body: Better an aruchah ("dish") of vegetables with love than a fattened ox with hatred. Aruchah means a simple ration or portion. Most families ate bread, lentils and vegetables, saving meat for festivals. Love can turn a cheap meal into a feast.

context.heading: The inner circle
context.body: Plans fail for lack of sod ("counsel"). Sod means more than advice; it is a close circle of confidants, a council that sits together. Wise plans are tested among trusted voices, not drawn up alone and announced.

theology.title: Eyes in every place
theology.body: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, watching the evil and the good (v. 3). That is comfort to the oppressed and warning to the oppressor. Hebrews 4:13 says nothing in all creation is hidden from Him; everything is laid bare before His eyes.

theology.title: Prayer over performance
theology.body: The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, but the prayer of the upright is His delight (v. 8). God is not impressed by religious display without a right heart (1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6). He delights in honest prayer from people who walk with Him.

theology.title: Humility before honor
theology.body: The fear of the LORD teaches wisdom, and humility comes before honor (v. 33). Jesus lived this out: He humbled Himself to death on a cross, and God highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:8–9). In God's kingdom the path up always runs down first.

application.title: Lower the temperature
application.body: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger (v. 1). You cannot control someone else's anger, but you can stop adding fuel.
application.question: In your hardest relationship, what would a gentle answer sound like next time?

application.title: Your face speaks first
application.body: A joyful heart makes a cheerful face, and a cheerful look brings joy to others (vv. 13, 30). Your face is the first message people receive from you.
application.question: What does your face usually tell your family when you walk in the door?

application.title: Get counsel
application.body: Plans succeed with many advisers (v. 22). Asking for advice is not weakness; it is how good plans get tested before reality tests them.
application.question: What big decision are you making right now without asking anyone wise?

context.heading: Weighing the motives
context.body: All a man's ways seem pure to him, but the LORD takhan ("weighs") the spirit. Egyptian art pictured the dead having their heart weighed on scales. Proverbs brings the idea into daily life: God evaluates the why behind our actions, not just the what.

context.heading: The scales are His
context.body: Honest peles ("scales") and balances belong to the LORD; all the weights in the bag are His concern. Ancient kings claimed to guarantee fair weights in their markets. Here the LORD Himself claims the merchant's measuring tools.

context.heading: High before the fall
context.body: Pride goes before destruction. Ga'on ("pride") means height or majesty, and Scripture uses it for God's own majesty (Exodus 15:7). When people take for themselves the height that belongs to God alone, a fall is already on its way.

theology.title: Our plans, His purpose
theology.body: Man plans his way, but the LORD directs his steps (v. 9; see also v. 1). Christians have long debated how these fit together. Scripture affirms both real human choice and God's overruling purpose (Acts 4:27–28; Philippians 2:12–13), without explaining away either.

theology.title: Nothing escapes His rule
theology.body: The LORD has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of disaster (v. 4). This does not make God the author of evil. It means evil cannot slip outside His rule, as at the cross, where the worst evil was turned into salvation (Acts 2:23).

theology.title: A better kind of strength
theology.body: Better to be patient than a warrior, and one who rules his spirit than one who captures a city (v. 32). God's power often shows itself through restraint. When insulted, Christ did not retaliate but entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

application.title: Hold plans loosely
application.body: Plan, but leave room for God to redirect you (v. 9). An interruption may be the LORD directing your steps.
application.question: What recent interruption might God have been using to redirect you?

application.title: Motive check
application.body: Your ways seem pure to you, but God weighs the why (v. 2). We judge ourselves by our intentions and others by their actions.
application.question: What good thing are you doing for a not-so-good reason?

application.title: Rule your spirit
application.body: Self-control is a bigger victory than taking a city (v. 32). Most battles with anger are lost in the first ten seconds.
application.question: What usually happens in your first ten seconds when you get angry?

context.heading: Medicine for the bones
context.body: A joyful heart is good gehah ("medicine"), a word found only here in the Old Testament, meaning a cure. A crushed spirit, by contrast, dries up the bones. Ancient Israelites saw what modern research keeps confirming: emotional and physical health are bound together.

context.heading: Declaring the guilty righteous
context.body: Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous are both detestable to the LORD. Tsadaq ("acquit") means to declare someone righteous in court. Judges in Israel were forbidden to take bribes or twist justice (Deuteronomy 16:19).

context.heading: The lucky stone
context.body: A shochad ("bribe") is a charm to the one who gives it, literally a "stone of favor," like a lucky charm. Verse 8 describes how bribery feels to the briber: it seems to open every door. Verse 23 tells what God thinks of it.

theology.title: God justifies the ungodly
theology.body: Verse 15 calls declaring the wicked righteous an abomination. Yet Paul says God "justifies the ungodly" (Romans 4:5). The cross resolves the tension: Christ bore the penalty, so God remains just while justifying those who believe in Jesus (Romans 3:26).

theology.title: Fire that refines
theology.body: The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but the LORD tests hearts (v. 3). Refining fire removes impurity; it does not destroy the metal. Peter applies this to trials that prove faith genuine, more precious than gold (1 Peter 1:7).

theology.title: He takes the poor personally
theology.body: Whoever mocks the poor insults their Maker (v. 5), repeating the thought of 14:31. God takes the treatment of the poor personally because they bear His image. Gloating over someone's disaster, the verse adds, will not go unpunished.

application.title: Peace over plenty
application.body: A dry crust with quiet beats a house full of feasting with strife (v. 1). A bigger house or a nicer vacation will not fix a home full of tension.
application.question: What are you upgrading in your life while the real problem stays the same?

application.title: Friends for the tight places
application.body: A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity (v. 17). Tsarah ("adversity") is a tight place; true friendship is tested when life closes in.
application.question: Who in your life is in a tight place right now, and how can you show up for them?

application.title: Silence as wisdom
application.body: Even a fool is considered wise when he keeps silent (v. 28). Not every thought needs to be posted or said.
application.question: Where would your silence do more good than your opinion this week?

context.heading: Delicious morsels
context.body: The words of a gossip are like mitlahamim ("choice morsels"), from a verb meaning to gulp down greedily. They go down into the inmost parts. Gossip tastes good when you hear it, and once swallowed it is not easily forgotten; it sinks in.

context.heading: Cutting yourself off
context.body: One who parad ("isolates") himself pursues his own desires and rebels against sound judgment. In a close-knit village, cutting yourself off from family and neighbors meant cutting yourself off from correction and help. Isolation is rarely as neutral as it feels.

context.heading: A wall made of imagination
context.body: The rich man thinks his wealth is a high wall, but only in his maskit ("imagination"). The word means an image or picture. His security is a picture he has painted for himself, not a wall that will stand when trouble comes.

theology.title: Calling on His name
theology.body: Verse 10 makes God's name a place to run. Joel promised that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved (Joel 2:32), and Paul applies that to calling on Jesus as Lord (Romans 10:13). The tower is open to anyone who runs to it.

theology.title: The friend who stays
theology.body: There is a friend who sticks closer than a brother (v. 24). Jesus calls His disciples friends and laid down His life for them (John 15:13–15). He promises, "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5), the loyalty this proverb describes.

theology.title: God hears both sides
theology.body: The first to plead his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him (v. 17). God is the Judge of all the earth who always does right (Genesis 18:25), because He hears everything. Human judges must imitate Him by listening fully before deciding.

application.title: Listen first
application.body: Answering before listening is folly and shame (v. 13). Most of us start writing our reply while the other person is still talking.
application.question: Who do you tend to interrupt, and what are you missing because of it?

application.title: Isolation is not neutral
application.body: Pulling away from people can feel like rest, but verse 1 warns that it can feed selfish desire. Alone too long, you lose the voices that keep you honest.
application.question: Who has stopped hearing from you lately, and why?

application.title: Words have weight
application.body: Death and life are in the power of the tongue (v. 21). Every text, comment and conversation either builds up or tears down.
application.question: Which of your words this week might someone still remember next year?

context.heading: Raging at God
context.body: A man's own folly ruins his life, yet his heart za'aph ("rages") against the LORD. The word pictures a stormy, sullen anger. Wrecked by his own choices, he blames God. The pattern is as old as Adam: "The woman You gave me" (Genesis 3:12).

context.heading: The council that stands
context.body: Many plans are in a man's heart, but the LORD's etsah ("purpose") will stand. The same word is used for a king's counsel or plan of action. God's counsel is the final word in heaven's throne room: "My purpose will stand" (Isaiah 46:10).

context.heading: Too lazy to eat
context.body: The sluggard buries his hand in the tsallachat ("dish") and will not even bring it back to his mouth. Ancient meals were eaten by hand from a shared bowl. The picture is deliberately comic: he is too lazy to feed himself.

theology.title: God puts Himself in debt
theology.body: Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay (v. 17). God puts Himself in the borrower's place. Jesus says what we do for the least we do for Him (Matthew 25:40), and that the measure we give will be measured back (Luke 6:38).

theology.title: God is not to blame
theology.body: Verse 3 shows people blaming God for their own folly. James 1:13 says no one should claim to be tempted by God, for God tempts no one. His goodness is not undone by our bad choices, and He stands ready to forgive them.

theology.title: Gifts only God can give
theology.body: House and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD (v. 14). Some gifts cannot be bought or inherited; they come straight from God's hand. Every good and perfect gift is from above (James 1:17).

application.title: Zeal without knowledge
application.body: Desire without knowledge is not good, and hurrying feet miss the way (v. 2). Passion is good, but rushing ahead without thinking does damage.
application.question: What are you rushing into with enthusiasm but little understanding?

application.title: Let it pass
application.body: It is a person's glory to overlook an offense (v. 11). Not every slight needs a response, a subtweet or a cold shoulder.
application.question: What offense are you holding onto that you could let pass today?

application.title: Owning your part
application.body: When our choices go badly, it is tempting to be angry at God (v. 3). Owning our share of the mess is where wisdom begins.
application.question: Where are you angry at God for a situation you helped create?

context.heading: Who can say "I am clean"?
context.body: "Who can say, 'I have kept my heart pure; I am cleansed from my sin'?" The verb zakah means to make clean or innocent. The question expects the answer: no one. Solomon himself prayed, "There is no one who does not sin" (1 Kings 8:46).

context.heading: Rash dedication
context.body: It is a trap to dedicate something as qodesh ("holy") rashly and only later consider the vows. Israelites could dedicate property to God by vow (Leviticus 27). Making the promise in a burst of feeling and rethinking it afterward was a snare.

context.heading: Waiting with tension
context.body: "Do not say, 'I will avenge this evil!' Wait on the LORD." Qavah ("wait") is related to the word for a cord, and pictures waiting stretched tight with expectation. It is active trust, letting God be the one who settles accounts.

theology.title: No one is pure
theology.body: Verse 9 asks who can claim a clean heart. Paul answers that all have sinned (Romans 3:23), and John adds that if we claim to be without sin we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). The good news starts with that honest diagnosis, then offers cleansing (1 John 1:9).

theology.title: God searches within
theology.body: The human spirit is the lamp of the LORD, searching every inner part (v. 27). David prayed, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalm 139:23). God's searching is not a threat to those who want to be known and healed.

theology.title: Vengeance belongs to God
theology.body: Verse 22 tells us to wait for the LORD, and He will save. Paul quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 with the same idea: "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay" (Romans 12:19). God's justice frees us from the exhausting job of settling every score ourselves.

application.title: Sweet now, gravel later
application.body: Bread gained by fraud tastes sweet, but afterward the mouth is full of gravel (v. 17). The pleasure of cutting corners fades quickly; the consequences stay.
application.question: What shortcut tasted good at first but has left you chewing gravel?

application.title: Yes said too fast
application.body: Verse 25 warns against hasty vows. Signing up, saying yes or making promises in an emotional moment can trap you later.
application.question: What yes did you give too quickly that you now need to deal with honestly?

application.title: What you reach for
application.body: Wine is a mocker (v. 1). Christians differ on whether to drink, but Scripture is clear that no substance should lead us astray.
application.question: What do you reach for when you want to escape, and is it starting to lead you?

context.heading: A corner of the roof
context.body: Better to live on a pinnah ("corner") of the roof than share a house with a quarrelsome wife. Israelite roofs were flat and used as living space, but a corner up there meant sun, wind and rain. The saying applies just as well to a quarrelsome husband.

context.heading: Worship with a scheme
context.body: The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, how much more when brought with zimmah ("evil intent"). Zimmah is a planned scheme. Bringing a gift to God to cover or advance a plot turns worship itself into an offense.

context.heading: The cry God hears
context.body: Whoever shuts his ears to the ze'aqah ("cry") of the poor will himself cry out and not be answered. The same word describes Israel's outcry in Egypt, which God heard (Exodus 3:7–9). Refusing to hear the poor puts you at odds with how God Himself acts.

theology.title: Ruler over rulers
theology.body: The king's heart is in the LORD's hand (v. 1). God moved the heart of Cyrus to free the exiles (Ezra 1:1) and sets up and removes kings (Daniel 2:21). No president, CEO or tyrant is beyond His reach. That is why Paul urges prayer for all in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

theology.title: Doing right over ritual
theology.body: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice (v. 3). The prophets said the same (Micah 6:6–8), and Jesus quoted Hosea to the religious leaders: "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" (Matthew 9:13). God wants lives, not just offerings.

theology.title: No wisdom against Him
theology.body: No wisdom, no understanding and no plan can succeed against the LORD (v. 30). Psalm 2 shows the nations plotting against the LORD and His Anointed while God laughs. The early church prayed that psalm when threatened (Acts 4:25–28), trusting that God's purposes cannot be overturned.

application.title: Prepare and trust
application.body: Verse 31 does not say skip preparing the horse. It says prepare well, then leave the outcome with God.
application.question: Where are you either refusing to prepare or refusing to trust?

application.title: Being right, being miserable
application.body: Verses 9 and 19 are blunt: constant quarreling makes a home unlivable. You can be right on every point and still make a house miserable.
application.question: What argument at home is more about winning than about the issue?

application.title: The cost of pleasure
application.body: Whoever loves pleasure will become poor (v. 17). Enjoyment is a gift, but chasing it drains both wallets and lives.
application.question: What pleasure are you spending more on than you can afford, in money or in time?

context.heading: Skilled hands
context.body: Do you see a man mahir ("skilled") in his work? The word means quick or ready, and Ezra is called a scribe skilled in the law (Ezra 7:6). Competence opens doors: such a person will serve before kings, not before obscure men.

context.heading: God takes the case
context.body: Do not rob the poor, for the LORD will riv ("take up") their case. Riv is a courtroom word for bringing a lawsuit. God appears as the legal defender of those who cannot afford one, and He takes the life of those who plunder them (v. 23).

context.heading: Debt as real slavery
context.body: The borrower is eved ("servant" or "slave") to the lender. In Israel, unpaid debts could lead to actual slavery, as when a creditor came to take a widow's two sons (2 Kings 4:1). The proverb describes a real legal danger, not just a figure of speech.

theology.title: Maker of rich and poor
theology.body: Rich and poor have this in common: the LORD is the Maker of them all (v. 2). Status differences are real but not ultimate. James 2:1–5 warns believers not to favor the rich in church, since God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith.

theology.title: All wisdom under God
theology.body: The words of the wise open by stating their aim: "so that your trust may be in the LORD" (v. 19). Whatever sources Israel's teachers drew on, Scripture places every piece of wisdom under God. All truth is His, and He puts it to work in the service of trusting Him.

theology.title: Training and grace
theology.body: "Train up a child in the way he should go" (v. 6). Christians differ on whether this is a promise or a general principle; many faithful parents have watched a child wander. Either way, the father in Jesus' parable kept watching the road (Luke 15:20), and grace is not limited by a parent's success.

application.title: Debt chains
application.body: The borrower is slave to the lender (v. 7). Monthly payments quietly limit your choices and add stress you carry everywhere.
application.question: What purchase on credit is still controlling your choices today?

application.title: Name over money
application.body: A good name is better than great riches (v. 1). Integrity takes years to build and moments to lose.
application.question: If your reputation rested only on what you do when no one is watching, what would it be?

application.title: Anger is contagious
application.body: Do not befriend an angry man, or you will learn his ways (vv. 24–25). Spend enough time with someone's temper and it becomes yours.
application.question: Whose anger are you absorbing, and how is it changing you?

context.heading: Worn out for money
context.body: Do not yaga ("wear yourself out") to get rich. The verb means to toil to exhaustion. The wise know when to stop, and verse 5 explains why: wealth can sprout wings and fly off like an eagle into the sky.

context.heading: There is a future
context.body: There is surely an acharit ("future") for you, and your hope will not be cut off. Acharit means the end or final outcome of something. The one who fears the LORD may watch sinners prosper for now, but the last chapter belongs to God.

context.heading: Give me your heart
context.body: "My son, give me your lev ("heart")." In Hebrew the heart is the center of thinking, choosing and desiring. The father asks not for outward compliance but for the inner allegiance that will keep his son from the traps described next.

theology.title: Father to the fatherless
theology.body: God's concern for orphans runs through Scripture: He is "a father to the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5) and calls His people to care for them (James 1:27). Through Christ, God adopts people who had no claim on Him at all (Galatians 4:4–7).

theology.title: God wants the heart
theology.body: The father's plea in verse 26 echoes God's own. "Love the LORD your God with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5) was the command Jesus called the greatest (Matthew 22:37). God is never satisfied with behavior alone; He wants the person.

theology.title: Envy fades in God's presence
theology.body: Do not let your heart envy sinners, but always continue in the fear of the LORD (v. 17). Psalm 73 tells how envy of the wicked faded when the psalmist entered God's sanctuary and saw their end. God's justice and our hope run on a longer horizon.

application.title: Exhausted for something fragile
application.body: Riches can sprout wings and fly away (v. 5). Wearing yourself out for something that fragile makes little sense.
application.question: What are you sacrificing your health or family for that could disappear overnight?

application.title: The cycle
application.body: Verse 35 ends with the drunkard saying, "When can I wake up to search for another drink?" Addiction means knowing it hurts and going back anyway.
application.question: What do you keep returning to even though you know it is hurting you?

application.title: Envy on a screen
application.body: Envying sinners (v. 17) is easy when their success scrolls past all day. Comparison steals contentment one post at a time.
application.question: Whose life do you find yourself envying, and what does that reveal about what you really want?

context.heading: Step in
context.body: Natsal ("rescue") those being led away to death. The same verb is used for God rescuing Israel from Egypt. The proverb calls for active intervention when someone is unjustly condemned or in danger, not quiet observation from a safe distance.

context.heading: No party at their fall
context.body: Do not samach ("gloat") when your enemy falls. The verb normally means to rejoice, the joy of a festival. Celebrating another's disaster is dangerous: the LORD may see it, disapprove and turn His anger away from them (v. 18).

context.heading: Those given to change
context.body: Fear the LORD and the king, and do not associate with the shanah ("rebellious"), literally "those who change." It probably means people who stir up revolt. In a world where coups usually brought bloodshed, the wise stayed clear of plotters.

theology.title: He repays by deeds
theology.body: "Will He not repay a man according to his deeds?" (v. 12). Paul echoes this in Romans 2:6. God's judgment is fair because it rests on what He sees in the heart, not on the excuses we offer.

theology.title: Falling and rising
theology.body: A righteous man may fall seven times and still get up (v. 16). Falling is expected; staying down is not. The LORD upholds all who fall (Psalm 145:14), and Jesus restored Peter after his three denials (John 21:15–19).

theology.title: Love for enemies
theology.body: Verses 17–18 forbid gloating over an enemy's fall. Jesus took this further: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44). God shows the pattern Himself; He sends rain on the just and the unjust.

application.title: "We didn't know"
application.body: Verse 12 says "we didn't know" is not an excuse God accepts. Sometimes ignorance is simply a choice not to look.
application.question: What injustice nearby have you chosen not to look into?

application.title: Get back up
application.body: Falling seven times is not the end (v. 16). Failure is part of the righteous life; quitting is optional.
application.question: What failure are you letting define you instead of rising again?

application.title: Slow ruin
application.body: Verses 33–34 repeat 6:10–11: a little sleep, and poverty arrives. The ruined vineyard took years, not one bad day.
application.question: What area of your life is slowly being overrun because you keep putting it off?

context.heading: Apples of gold
context.body: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in maskit ("settings") of silver. Maskit means a carved image or ornament. The picture is fine jewelry or decorative metalwork: the right word, in the right setting, is a work of art.

context.heading: Coals on his head
context.body: Feeding your enemy heaps gechalim ("burning coals") on his head. The meaning is debated: some point to an Egyptian ritual of carrying coals as a sign of repentance, others to the burning shame that kindness produces. Either way, the aim is a changed enemy, not a humiliated one.

context.heading: A city without walls
context.body: Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who lacks ma'tsar ("self-control"). Walls were a city's defense; without them it lay open to every raider. A person without restraint is defenseless against every passing impulse.

theology.title: Kindness to enemies
theology.body: Paul quotes verses 21–22 in Romans 12:20 to show how to overcome evil with good. Jesus commands love for enemies (Matthew 5:44), and God did it first: while we were His enemies, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son (Romans 5:10).

theology.title: Humility at the table
theology.body: Do not exalt yourself before the king; it is better to be told, "Come up here" (vv. 6–7). Jesus built a parable on this saying (Luke 14:8–11): everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. God's kingdom overturns human status games.

theology.title: Refined for use
theology.body: Remove the dross from the silver, and a vessel comes out for the silversmith (v. 4). God purifies His people to make them useful, refining them like silver (Malachi 3:3), so they can be vessels for honorable use (2 Timothy 2:21).

application.title: Right word, right time
application.body: A word fitly spoken is beautiful (v. 11). Timing and tone matter as much as content.
application.question: What true thing do you need to say, and when would be the right moment?

application.title: Don't overstay
application.body: Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, or he will grow tired of you (v. 17). Even good relationships need breathing room.
application.question: Where might you be wearing out your welcome?

application.title: Walls down
application.body: Without self-control you are a city without walls (v. 28). Every craving finds the gate open.
application.question: Which wall in your life needs rebuilding first?

context.heading: Back to the vomit
context.body: As a dog returns to its qe ("vomit"), so a fool repeats his folly. Dogs in the ancient world were scavengers, not pets. Peter quotes this proverb about people who return to corruption after knowing the way of righteousness (2 Peter 2:22).

context.heading: A cheap pot with a shiny glaze
context.body: Burning lips and a wicked heart are like kesef ("glaze," literally "silver") over an earthen vessel. Potters could coat cheap clay with a shiny silver-dross glaze to make it look valuable. Warm words can cover a cheap, cracked heart.

context.heading: Turning on its hinges
context.body: As a door turns on its hinges, so the sluggard turns on his bed (v. 14). Ancient doors swung on a post set into stone sockets: plenty of motion, no progress. The sluggard rolls over again and again but never gets anywhere.

theology.title: Wisdom needs discernment
theology.body: Verses 4–5 show that God's wisdom is not a rulebook to apply mechanically. He gave a Scripture that requires us to think, pray and grow in discernment (Hebrews 5:14). Jesus sometimes answered His critics and sometimes declined to (Mark 11:29–33).

theology.title: The pit you dig
theology.body: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it (v. 27). God built a moral order where evil often backfires on its author. Haman was hanged on the very gallows he built for Mordecai (Esther 7:10), and Psalm 7:15–16 makes the same point.

theology.title: He sees through disguises
theology.body: Verses 24–28 describe hatred hidden behind gracious speech. God is not fooled. Jesus quoted Isaiah against those who honor God with their lips while their hearts are far from Him (Matthew 15:8), and He knew what was in every person (John 2:25).

application.title: When to engage
application.body: Verses 4–5 put two opposite instructions side by side. Some arguments need a response; most online ones do not. Wisdom is knowing the difference.
application.question: Which argument are you in right now that you should simply drop?

application.title: Not your fight
application.body: Meddling in someone else's quarrel is like grabbing a dog by the ears (v. 17). You get bitten, and you cannot easily let go.
application.question: What fight have you jumped into that was never yours?

application.title: "Just kidding"
application.body: Like a madman shooting deadly arrows is the one who deceives his neighbor and says, "I was only joking!" (vv. 18–19). Humor can be a cover for cruelty.
application.question: When have you hidden a real dig behind the words "just kidding"?

context.heading: Tested by applause
context.body: The matsreph ("crucible") is for silver and the furnace for gold, and a man is tested by the praise he receives. Praise exposes what is in a person the way heat exposes impurities in metal. How you handle applause shows your heart.

context.heading: Misplaced praise
context.body: Do not halal ("boast") about tomorrow. Halal is the root of hallelujah, "praise the LORD." Boasting is praise turned the wrong way, aimed at yourself and your plans instead of at God, who alone knows what a day will bring.

context.heading: Never full
context.body: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and neither are human eyes. Abaddon, "destruction," names the realm of the dead. Like the grave, human desire keeps taking in and never says, "Enough." Advertising is built on that hunger: there is always one more thing to see, own or try.

theology.title: God holds tomorrow
theology.body: You do not know what a day may bring (v. 1). James 4:13–15 builds on this: instead of boasting, say, "If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that." Only God sees tomorrow, and He is trustworthy with it.

theology.title: Only God satisfies
theology.body: Human eyes are never satisfied (v. 20). Ecclesiastes 1:8 says the eye never has enough of seeing. Jesus offers water that ends thirst for good (John 4:13–14), and the psalmist finds fullness of joy in God's presence (Psalm 16:11).

theology.title: Wounds from a loving hand
theology.body: The wounds of a friend can be trusted (v. 6). God's correction is the truest of these: "Those I love, I rebuke and discipline" (Revelation 3:19). Like a friend's honest wound, His rebukes come from loyalty, never from contempt, and they aim to bring us back, not drive us away.

application.title: Let others do it
application.body: Let another praise you, and not your own mouth (v. 2). Self-promotion is built into much of online life.
application.question: What do you post or say mainly so others will think well of you?

application.title: The neighbor next door
application.body: A neighbor nearby is better than a brother far away (v. 10). In a crisis, distance matters.
application.question: Do you know your neighbors well enough to ask them for help, and if not, what is one step toward that?

application.title: Check your flocks
application.body: Know the condition of your flocks (v. 23). For most of us that means finances, health and relationships we have stopped checking on.
application.question: Which of your "flocks" have you not looked at closely in months?

context.heading: Two kinds of covering
context.body: Whoever kasah ("conceals") his sins will not prosper. It is the same verb as 10:12, where love covers wrongs. Covering others' sins in love is good; covering your own to escape responsibility is ruinous. The same act, hiding a wrong, is either mercy or self-protection depending on whose wrong it is.

context.heading: Prayer that ignores God's word
context.body: If anyone turns his ear from hearing torah ("the law"), even his prayer is detestable. Torah means instruction, God's revealed teaching. Prayer that refuses to listen to God has become a monologue. Isaiah 1:15 gives the same warning: God will not listen to people whose prayers come from hands they refuse to wash.

context.heading: A tender conscience
context.body: Blessed is the man who is always pachad ("reverent"), literally "trembling." Here the trembling is healthy: a conscience sensitive before God. The second line contrasts it with the person who hardens his heart and falls into trouble.

theology.title: Mercy for confessors
theology.body: Whoever confesses and renounces his sins will find mercy (v. 13). David knew this: when he kept silent his bones wasted away, but when he confessed, God forgave (Psalm 32:3–5). John promises the same: if we confess, He is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9).

theology.title: Seeking brings understanding
theology.body: Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it fully (v. 5). Moral clarity comes from relationship with God. Paul says the spiritual person can discern what others cannot (1 Corinthians 2:14–15).

theology.title: Rulers under the law
theology.body: A ruler who lacks judgment is a great oppressor (v. 16). God holds leaders to His law; Israel's kings were to copy it and read it daily so they would not think themselves above their brothers (Deuteronomy 17:18–20).

application.title: Secrets cost
application.body: Concealing sin will not prosper (v. 13). Secrets take energy to keep and slowly corrode relationships.
application.question: What are you hiding that you need to confess to God, and maybe to one trusted person?

application.title: Honest over pleasant
application.body: Whoever rebukes a man will in the end gain more favor than one who flatters (v. 23). Honest friends are rare and valuable.
application.question: Who needs your honest word more than your compliments right now?

application.title: Hurry to get rich
application.body: One who hurries to get rich will not go unpunished (v. 20). Haste tends to cut corners and miss danger.
application.question: Where is your hurry to get ahead leading you to cut corners?

context.heading: The snare of fear
context.body: The fear of man is a moqesh ("snare"), a trap for birds. The word for fear, charadah, means trembling. Worry about people's opinions works like a snare: it catches quietly, holds tightly and keeps you from moving freely.

context.heading: A neck like an ox
context.body: A man who qashah ("hardens") his neck after many rebukes will suddenly be shattered. Stiff-necked describes an ox refusing the yoke, and God used it of Israel at the golden calf (Exodus 32:9). The verse uses the same word for "rebuke" found in 1:23, where Wisdom's warnings were refused.

context.heading: Stilling the storm
context.body: A fool gives full vent to his anger, but a wise man shavach ("holds it back"). The verb means to soothe or still, and it is used of God stilling the sea's rising waves (Psalm 89:9).

theology.title: Trust over fear
theology.body: The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high (v. 25). Jesus told His disciples not to fear those who can kill the body (Matthew 10:28). Paul said that if he were still trying to please people, he would not be Christ's servant (Galatians 1:10).

theology.title: Justice comes from the LORD
theology.body: Many seek a ruler's favor, but justice for a man comes from the LORD (v. 26). Human courts and bosses fail; God's justice is final. He has established His throne for judgment and will judge the world in righteousness (Psalm 9:7–8).

theology.title: Patience with a limit
theology.body: Verse 1 describes many warnings before sudden ruin. God is patient, not wanting anyone to perish (2 Peter 3:9). But His patience is meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4), not to give us more time to harden.

application.title: People-pleasing
application.body: Fear of others' opinions traps you (v. 25). It quietly shapes what you say, buy, wear and post.
application.question: Whose disapproval do you fear most, and how is it steering your choices?

application.title: Venting is not wisdom
application.body: A fool gives full vent to his anger (v. 11). Venting feels like release, but it usually leaves damage behind for others to clean up.
application.question: Where do you need to hold back instead of saying everything you feel?

application.title: Repeated warnings
application.body: Verse 1 describes someone who ignored correction many times. The same warning repeated is often God's mercy.
application.question: What warning have you heard more than once that you keep ignoring?

context.heading: Give, give
context.body: The aluqah ("leech") has two daughters: "Give! Give!" Leeches feed through suckers at both ends. Agur uses the image to picture appetite that never stops, then lists four things never satisfied: the grave, the barren womb, dry land and fire (vv. 15–16).

context.heading: Small but wise
context.body: Shaphan ("rock badgers"), the hyrax, are small and weak, yet they make their homes in the cliffs. Agur lists four small creatures: ants, hyraxes, locusts and lizards. Their wisdom is knowing their limits and using the protection and order available to them.

context.heading: "What is his son's name?"
context.body: Agur asks who has gone up to heaven and come down, and "what is His name, and the name of His ben ("son")?" The question points to the mystery of God. Many Christians hear an echo in John 3:13, where Jesus says He came down from heaven.

theology.title: Do not add to His words
theology.body: Every word of God is flawless, so do not add to His words, or He will rebuke you (vv. 5–6). Deuteronomy 4:2 and Revelation 22:18–19 give the same warning. God's word does not need our improvements, only our trust.

theology.title: The humble mind
theology.body: Agur confesses he lacks understanding and has not learned wisdom (vv. 2–3). True wisdom begins with knowing your limits. God is far beyond us (Job 38–42), and Jesus thanked the Father for revealing His truth to little children rather than the proud (Matthew 11:25).

theology.title: Daily bread
theology.body: "Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion" (v. 8). Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread (Matthew 6:11). God provides enough, and contentment is something learned in every circumstance (Philippians 4:11–12).

application.title: Enough
application.body: Agur fears riches would make him forget God and poverty would tempt him to steal (v. 9). Both extremes threaten faith.
application.question: What would "enough" look like for you, and are you aiming at it?

application.title: Appetite that grows
application.body: The leech always wants more (v. 15). Some appetites grow the more you feed them.
application.question: Which appetite in your life keeps asking for more?

application.title: Wise in small things
application.body: The small creatures are wise because they know their limits (vv. 24–28). Strength is not the only path to thriving.
application.question: Where would admitting your limits make you wiser?

context.heading: Charm and breath
context.body: Charm is sheqer ("deceptive") and beauty is hevel ("fleeting"), literally breath or vapor. Charm can hide what is underneath, and beauty fades like breath on a cold morning. The fear of the LORD lasts, and the book ends where it began (1:7).

context.heading: Laughing at tomorrow
context.body: She sachaq ("laughs") at the days to come, the same verb used of Wisdom rejoicing at creation (8:30). Her preparation gives her freedom from fear of the future, and her household is clothed even for snow (v. 21).

context.heading: Dressed for battle
context.body: She chagar ("girds") herself with strength. Girding meant tucking long robes into a belt for hard work or for battle. The language of the poem is almost military: this is a warrior in her household.

theology.title: Wisdom with a home address
theology.body: Lady Wisdom built her house in chapter 9; this woman builds her household in chapter 31. The book ends by showing wisdom lived out in ordinary days: trading, planting, sewing, giving and teaching. The fear of the LORD bookends the whole book (1:7; 31:30).

theology.title: God's heart for the voiceless
theology.body: "Open your mouth for those with no voice" (v. 8). God defends the weak and the fatherless (Psalm 82:3–4). Jesus opened His ministry with Isaiah's words about good news to the poor and freedom for the oppressed (Luke 4:18).

theology.title: Ordinary faithfulness counts
theology.body: Her worth is far above rubies (v. 10), the same value given to wisdom itself (3:15; 8:11). God prizes faithful everyday work as much as public greatness. Jesus noticed a widow's two small coins when others saw only the big gifts (Mark 12:41–44).

application.title: Not a checklist
application.body: This poem is often read as an impossible to-do list for women. It is better read as a picture of wise living that honors work, generosity and faith, qualities meant for everyone.
application.question: Which quality in this poem do you most want growing in your life?

application.title: Speak for someone
application.body: Lemuel's mother tells him to speak up for those who cannot (v. 8). Power, platform and influence exist to protect others.
application.question: Who around you needs someone to speak up for them?

application.title: What lasts
application.body: Charm deceives and beauty fades (v. 30). We often pour the most into what lasts the least.
application.question: What are you investing in now that will still matter in twenty years?
